0.title: Strength for the Sake of Others
0.essay:
Few questions confuse our generation more than this one: what does it mean to be a man? The Bible answers by pointing not to a stereotype but to a person.

Three confusions

Some voices say manhood is about dominance, toughness and conquest, and that real men never show weakness. Others say manhood is an outdated idea, that talk of male strength is dangerous, and that the differences between men and women are only what society has taught us. Meanwhile many men simply drift. They avoid responsibility, retreat into screens and entertainment, and leave the hard work of leading, protecting and building to someone else.

A gift and a calling

The Bible starts somewhere else. Manhood is not something a man invents, proves or earns. It is a gift and a calling from God. “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). Men and women stand side by side as equal bearers of God’s image, equal in dignity and equal heirs of grace. And God made them different on purpose, so that together they reflect his goodness in ways neither could alone.

Manhood in a person

Most of all, the Bible shows us manhood in Jesus Christ, the true man, who lived as Adam should have lived. In him we see strength without cruelty and tenderness without weakness. He drove the money-changers out of the temple and took little children in his arms. He faced a mob to protect his friends, wept at a friend’s grave and washed his disciples’ feet. He said, “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), yet he is also “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5).

A simple summary may help: biblical manhood is strength used for the good of others under the lordship of Christ. A godly man receives his life as a gift, works and guards what God has entrusted to him, protects and provides, leads by serving, and loves as Christ loved.

Where these studies stand

These studies follow the historic Reformed understanding usually called complementarian: men and women are equal in worth, but God has given them distinct and complementary callings, especially in marriage and in the leadership of the church. Many sincere Christians, usually called egalitarians, read some of the key passages differently. Where those questions arise, the other view is explained fairly.

These studies are not only for married men. Jesus never married, and Paul was single throughout his ministry. Every man, married or single, young or old, is called to live out his manhood before God.

Grace, not guilt

This is not a checklist for proving yourself. Every man who reads these pages has failed as a man in some way, often deeply. The good news is that Christ came for failed men. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Biblical manhood grows out of grace, not guilt.

The chapters

Made in God’s Image; Adam’s Calling and Adam’s Failure; Jesus, the True Man; Leading by Serving in the home; The Man in the Church and in the World; and Purity, Work and Finishing Well.

For reflection

What messages about manhood did you absorb growing up, from family, friends or culture? Which of them fit the Bible, and which do not?

1.title: Made in God's Image: Equal and Different
1.essay:
The story of manhood does not begin with men. It begins with God, who made humanity in his own image, male and female.

The image of God

“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). Notice the rhythm: three times the verse says God created. The making of humanity is the climax of the whole account. To bear God’s image means to represent him, to reflect his character and to rule the world on his behalf, like a king’s statue that shows who owns the land.

The word man here means humanity as a whole, and the verse immediately tells us that humanity comes in two forms. God did not make man and then add woman as an afterthought. Both are there in the first description. Both reflect God, both are given dominion, both receive his blessing. And when God looked at everything he had made, “behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31).

Equal

So two things are true at once. First, men and women are equal. A man is not more human, more valuable or more in God’s image than a woman. Peter calls wives “heirs with you of the grace of life” (1 Peter 3:7). Paul says that “there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

Galatians 3:28 is sometimes used to argue that there are no differences at all. But Paul is not erasing the differences between Jew and Greek, slave and free, or male and female. He is saying that none of them affect our standing before God. Every believer is justified in exactly the same way and adopted into the same family. A Christian man may never think of himself as spiritually superior to a Christian woman. At the foot of the cross the ground is level. Any view of manhood that treats women as lesser, as objects, or as servants of male desire is not biblical manhood. It is sin.

Different

Second, men and women are different, and the difference is good. God did not make one kind of person and then divide it arbitrarily. He made a man and a woman, each with a distinct design, to fit together and complement one another: different bodies, different roles in bearing and raising children, and, as later chapters show, different callings in marriage and in church leadership. Paul holds both truths together: “Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God” (1 Corinthians 11:11–12).

Work it and keep it

Genesis 2 fills in the picture. Before there was a wife, a family, a nation or a church, God gave the man a job: he put him in the garden “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). The first word means cultivating, making the garden fruitful. The second means guarding, protecting what God had entrusted. These two callings run through the Bible’s whole picture of manhood. A godly man builds and he guards.

Work is not a result of the fall. It was part of paradise. What the fall did was make work frustrating (Genesis 3:17). The calling itself is good.

Not good to be alone

Then, for the first time in the Bible, God says something is not good: “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him” (Genesis 2:18). The word helper does not mean servant or inferior. God himself is called his people’s helper: “Behold, God is my helper” (Psalm 54:4).

For a man, this verse is humbling. He was not made to be self-sufficient. He was made for relationship and for responsibility, not to live for himself. He needs others, and in marriage he needs his wife. Even a single man needs the fellowship of the church. Isolation is not strength.

Received, not proved

The world tells men that manhood must be proved, by strength, money, sexual conquest or success. The Bible tells men that manhood is received from God. You do not become a man by winning, earning or dominating. You grow as a man by receiving God’s design and living it for his glory and the good of others. A man who knows he is made in God’s image and loved in Christ is free from the endless need to prove himself, and free to spend his strength on others.

Two errors

Just a few generations after Adam, Genesis shows us Lamech, the first man in the Bible to take two wives, boasting to them about killing a young man: “If Cain’s revenge is sevenfold, then Lamech’s is seventy-sevenfold” (Genesis 4:24). He is manhood turned into violence and pride. At the other extreme is Adam in the garden, standing silently while his wife was deceived. Every age produces both: the man who dominates and the man who disappears. Ours has plenty of each.

A simple test: when people are around you, do they feel safer or more afraid? Do the people under your influence flourish or shrink? Strength that makes others fearful is not biblical manhood. Strength that makes others safe, free and able to grow reflects the God who made us.

For reflection

What has God entrusted to you to build and to guard? Which error are you more prone to, dominating others or disappearing from responsibility, and what would repentance look like?

2.title: Adam's Calling and Adam's Failure
2.essay:
To understand what has gone wrong with men, we have to go back to the garden, and to a man who stood silent when he should have spoken.

The word entrusted

Before the woman was created, God gave the man a clear command: “You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat” (Genesis 2:16–17). Notice how generous God’s first words are. Only one tree was forbidden. The command was not a burden but a boundary that protected life.

Adam received God’s word first, and with it came the responsibility to hold on to it, to pass it on, and to protect the garden and his wife from anything that would lead them away from it. That does not mean Eve was less responsible to obey. But it suggests the man carried a particular responsibility to guard God’s word. Spiritual leadership is not a privilege to enjoy but a weight to carry. And it is still the heart of a godly man’s calling: not to make his own rules or live by his feelings, but to listen to what God has said, believe that God is good, and lead others to trust him too.

He was with her

Then the serpent came. It spoke to the woman, twisting God’s word and questioning his goodness. She was deceived and ate. And then comes one of the most painful phrases in the Bible: “she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate” (Genesis 3:6).

Adam was there. He was not away in the field. He heard the conversation. He did not step between his wife and the serpent. He did not remind her of God’s word. He stood silent, and then he followed her into sin. The tragedy of Adam is not only that he ate, but that he did nothing before he ate. His silence was a choice. Many of the worst failures of men are not loud acts of wickedness but quiet refusals to speak, to act and to protect when it mattered most.

Where are you?

When God came into the garden, he called first to the man: “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). In Hebrew the word you is singular. God held the man responsible. Although Eve ate first, the New Testament traces humanity’s fall to Adam: “sin came into the world through one man” (Romans 5:12). In Scripture, the one who leads is the one who answers for those he leads.

Yet God’s question was not a request for information. He knew where Adam was. It was an invitation, calling Adam out of hiding and into accountability. Even after Adam’s sin, God came looking for him. That is grace. God still calls to men who are hiding, in shame, in addiction, in busyness or in silence. The way back begins with an honest answer.

Passivity, then blame

Adam’s answer was to blame his wife, and even God: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3:12). Passivity, then blame. Men have been repeating that pattern ever since.

God named Adam’s sin precisely: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you” (Genesis 3:17). The problem was not that Adam listened to his wife. Wise husbands do. The problem was that he listened to her instead of God. And the result: “cursed is the ground because of you” (Genesis 3:17). The very place of his calling, his work, became painful. Men still feel that curse in frustration, failure and exhaustion. But in Christ the curse is broken, and work done for him is never in vain.

The curse on marriage

God told the woman, “Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16). The ESV notes that “for” may be read “against,” and points to Genesis 4:7, where sin’s desire is against Cain and he must rule over it. Many understand the curse to describe a struggle: the wife tempted to resist her husband’s leadership, the husband tempted to crush her. “He shall rule over you” describes what sin does to marriage, not what God designed it to be. Harsh male rule is a result of the fall, not a picture of godly manhood.

Adam’s sons today

Many Christian homes today have an Adam in them. He loves his family, but he leaves spiritual matters to his wife. She prays with the children, takes them to church, handles the hard conversations and makes the difficult decisions. He is present but passive. The world may call him easygoing. Genesis calls it Adam’s sin.

Other homes have the opposite problem. The man leads, but by anger, control and intimidation. His family walks on eggshells. He may even quote Bible verses about headship. But he is living out the curse, not the creation.

Both men need the same thing: to see themselves in Adam, to repent, and to look to the man who got it right. For God did not leave men in Adam’s failure. He sent another man.

For reflection

Where are you tempted to be present but passive, in your home, church or friendships? If God asked you today, “Where are you?”, what would an honest answer be?

3.title: Jesus, the True Man
3.essay:
If Adam shows us what went wrong with manhood, Jesus shows us what manhood was meant to be. He is the man who succeeded at every point where Adam failed.

The last Adam

Paul sets two men side by side. The first Adam received life from God. But “the last Adam became a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45). Christ gives life to others. Scripture presents these two as representative men: “For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

Every man is either in Adam or in Christ. So biblical manhood is not first about behaviour but about union with Christ. A man does not become godly by trying harder to be a better Adam. He becomes godly by being joined to Christ and receiving his life.

Two tests

Adam was tested in a garden full of food, and fell. Jesus was tested in a barren wilderness after forty days without food, and stood firm, answering Satan with God’s word: “Man shall not live by bread alone” (Luke 4:4).

Adam grasped at what God had forbidden. In another garden, Gethsemane, Jesus surrendered to what God had willed: “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).

Two gardens

Adam stood silent while his wife was deceived. When soldiers came to arrest Jesus, he stepped forward: “I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go” (John 18:8). He put himself between his friends and danger.

In Eden, a man stood silent while evil came for the one he should have protected. In Gethsemane, a man stepped forward and said, in effect, “Take me, and let them go.” Every Christian man lives between those two gardens. By nature we are Adam. By grace we are being made like Christ.

The breadth of his manhood

Look at the variety of Jesus’ manhood. He worked with his hands for years as a carpenter (Mark 6:3). He spoke with an authority that silenced his enemies. He was indignant when his disciples turned children away, “And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them” (Mark 10:16). He wept openly at the grave of his friend Lazarus. Many men have been taught that tears are weakness. Yet the strongest man who ever lived was not ashamed to grieve. Biblical manhood does not mean hiding every emotion. It means feeling rightly and acting faithfully.

Lord with a towel

On his last night, Jesus did a slave’s job. He washed the dusty feet of his disciples, including the one who would betray him. Then he explained: “If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you” (John 13:14–15).

Notice that he calls himself Lord and Teacher. He did not stop being Lord when he knelt. His authority was expressed in service. “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). In God’s kingdom, authority is measured by how much a man gives, not how much he gets. The husband, the father, the elder and the boss are not above the towel and the basin. The more authority a man has, the lower he should be willing to kneel.

Gentle and strong

Jesus invites weary people to come to him because of the kind of man he is: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). The world does not usually admire those qualities in men. But notice that he says this while calling people to take his yoke, to submit to his authority. He is a gentle King, not a weak one.

Gentleness is not weakness. It is strength held in check and used for the good of others. The same Jesus who is gentle with the broken is the conquering Lion of the tribe of Judah. A godly man is not either tough or tender. He is both, at the right time and in the right way. The men who are safest to be around are those who have learned from him.

He knows the fight

Jesus faced every temptation men face: to lust, to grasp at power, to give in to anger, to run from pain, to take the easy way. “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). He is not a distant example who cannot understand. When a man is struggling, he does not need to hide from Jesus. He can come to the one who knows the fight and has already won it.

Grace for failed men

And Jesus restores failed men. Peter denied him three times. After the resurrection, Jesus asked him three times whether he loved him, and then gave him a new calling: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). Jesus is not only our model. He is our Saviour. No man can copy him by effort alone. We need his forgiveness for our failures and his Spirit to make us like him.

For reflection

Jesus is both “gentle and lowly” and the Lion of Judah. Which do you most need to grow in? What would washing feet look like in your home, workplace or church this week?

4.title: Leading by Serving: The Man in His Home
4.essay:
Nowhere is a man’s character more clearly seen than at home. Colleagues and friends see our best. The people who live with us see the truth.

Headship defined by the cross

The central verse is this: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Paul does call the husband the head of his wife (Ephesians 5:23). But he immediately defines that headship by the cross. The husband’s model is not a king on a throne but a Saviour on a cross. His leadership is measured by his sacrifice.

Paul could have told husbands to love their wives as much as they are loved, or as much as they deserve. Instead he gives an impossible standard. Christ loved his bride when she was unlovely, unfaithful and far from him, and gave himself up for her all the way to death. A husband who takes this seriously will stop asking, “What am I getting out of this marriage?” and start asking, “What can I give?” And he will quickly discover that he cannot love like this in his own strength. He will need to go to the cross himself, for forgiveness and for power.

Not harsh

One of the shortest instructions to husbands is also one of the most searching: “Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them” (Colossians 3:19). Harshness can be loud, in anger and shouting, or quiet, in coldness, sarcasm, criticism and withdrawal. Paul names it because it is a particular temptation for men who carry responsibility and feel its pressure. A man can be faithful, hardworking and sexually pure, and still be harsh. God cares about the tone of a man’s home, not just its rules.

Peter adds that husbands are to “live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman” (1 Peter 3:7).

What a godly husband and father does

He leads spiritually. He takes responsibility for the spiritual health of his home, prays with and for his family, and brings them to God’s word.

He protects. He guards his family from harm, physical, emotional and spiritual. When Nehemiah’s builders were threatened, he told them, “Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes” (Nehemiah 4:14).

He provides. “But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). Those are some of the strongest words in the New Testament. Even people who do not know God usually care for their own. The verse does not condemn men who cannot work because of illness, disability or circumstances beyond their control. It condemns neglect. Where wives also work outside the home, as the capable woman of Proverbs 31 did, the husband’s responsibility to see that his household is cared for remains.

He nurtures his children. “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). The warning is against harshness, unfairness, constant criticism, broken promises, favouritism or neglect. The command is to train and to teach, and both are “of the Lord.” Fathers are not raising children in their own image but to know Christ. The goal is not merely well-behaved children, but children who love God.

Fathers as a picture of God

“As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him” (Psalm 103:13). Children often learn what God is like from their fathers. A father who is harsh, absent or unpredictable makes it harder for a child to trust the heavenly Father. A father who is present, patient and firm gives his children a living picture of God’s love.

Headship and equality

Paul writes that “the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3). Christ himself is under the headship of the Father, yet equal to him. So headship does not imply superior worth. It describes an order of responsibility and love, and a husband will answer to God for how he has led and loved his wife.

The two views

Christians disagree about how to understand headship. Complementarians, whose view these studies follow, believe God gives husbands a real, loving responsibility to lead, which wives are called to support. Egalitarians point to Ephesians 5:21, “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ,” and understand marriage as a partnership of mutual submission without a distinct leadership role for the husband.

Many complementarians read Ephesians 5:21 as the general call to humility that Paul then applies in particular relationships: wives and husbands, children and parents, servants and masters (Ephesians 5:22–6:9). In every case, the one with more responsibility is called to the greater self-giving. No Christian husband is exempt from humility. Both views agree on what matters most: a husband must love sacrificially, and no man may ever use Scripture to justify control or abuse.

Leadership on a Tuesday

Spiritual leadership rarely looks dramatic. It looks like a man who suggests praying together before bed, even when it feels awkward. A man who says, “I was wrong; please forgive me,” before his wife has to ask. A man who reads a Bible story with his children, gets the family to church when everyone is tired, notices when his wife is overwhelmed and takes something off her plate, and asks her what she thinks before a big decision. Leadership at home is mostly initiative, humility and consistency.

When headship is twisted

Tragically, some men use the Bible’s teaching on headship to control, intimidate or abuse their wives and children. This is a grievous sin against God and a lie about Christ, who never bullied his bride. Anyone living in an abusive home should seek safety and help, from church leaders and, where there is danger or crime, from the authorities. Headship never requires a wife or child to submit to abuse or to sin.

For reflection

In what forms, loud or quiet, might harshness show up in your home? If you are a father, what are your children learning about God from you? If you are single, how can you support the families in your church?

5.title: The Man in the Church and in the World
5.essay:
Near the end of his first letter to the Corinthians, Paul gives a compact summary of Christian manhood: “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love” (1 Corinthians 16:13–14).

Courage and love

Four short commands, and one that governs them all. Be watchful: stay spiritually alert. Stand firm in the faith: do not be moved from the truth. Act like men: take responsibility with courage, and do not be childish or cowardly. Be strong: persevere. Paul wrote this to the whole church, women included, but the phrase “act like men” shows that Scripture does connect courage and steadiness with manhood.

Then comes the last command: let all be done in love. Courage and love belong together. A man who is strong without love becomes a bully. A man who is loving without strength becomes useless when the truth is under attack.

Leadership in the church

The New Testament describes the office of elder or overseer, the pastors who shepherd and teach the church. Among the qualifications, an overseer must be “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2), which the ESV notes may be read “a man of one woman,” a man faithful in his sexual life.

Paul also writes, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man,” and he grounds this in creation: “For Adam was formed first, then Eve” (1 Timothy 2:12–13). This is one of the most debated passages in the New Testament, and it deserves careful, humble reading. Paul restricts two things, teaching men and exercising authority over men, most naturally understood in the setting of the gathered church and its leadership. He does not forbid women from teaching altogether. Older women are to teach younger women (Titus 2:3–4), and Priscilla helped explain the gospel to Apollos (Acts 18:26).

The two views

Complementarians, including the Reformed tradition historically, understand these passages to mean that the office of elder or pastor is reserved for qualified men, while women serve in many other vital ministries. Egalitarians often read Paul’s words as addressing a particular situation in Ephesus, such as false teaching spreading among untrained women, and believe women may serve in every office.

These studies follow the complementarian reading, because Paul roots his instruction in creation rather than local circumstances (1 Timothy 2:13; compare 1 Corinthians 11:8–9). His reason is not that women are less intelligent or less spiritual. It is the order God established. Christians on both sides love Scripture and seek to obey it.

Qualified, not merely male

The qualifications for elders (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9) are almost entirely about character: self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, managing his household well. Being male is not enough. The church does not need more men in charge. It needs more godly men who serve. For men, the creation-order passages are not a trophy but a trust. If God calls qualified men to shepherd his church, they must do it as servants who will give an account.

Every man serves

Most men will never be elders. But every Christian man is called to serve. Paul’s instruction for younger men is strikingly simple: “urge the younger men to be self-controlled” (Titus 2:6). Self-control is the virtue young men most need and most lack: control of anger, appetite, sexual desire, tongue and time. Then he tells Titus, “Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works” (Titus 2:7). Young men learn by watching older men. Every Christian man is teaching someone, whether he means to or not.

Christianity spreads through such relationships: “what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). A mature Christian man is not only a learner but a trainer of others.

Brothers who sharpen

“Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17). When two blades are rubbed together, both become sharper, and friction is part of the process. Real friendship between men includes honest conversation, disagreement, rebuke and encouragement. Deep friendship between men is a gift from God: “the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (1 Samuel 18:1).

Many men have plenty of acquaintances and no real friends. They talk about sport, work and the news, but no one knows their fears, temptations or doubts. Isolation makes men vulnerable to sin and despair. A practical step: find one or two Christian men and meet regularly to read Scripture, pray and ask each other honest questions.

Courage in public

Christian men are to be salt and light in the world: honest at work, courageous for the weak and faithful in their witness. Proverbs calls a ruler to “Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute” (Proverbs 31:8). Christian men are called to use their strength for those who cannot defend themselves: the unborn, the poor, the abused, the overlooked colleague, the bullied child. Biblical manhood is not loud self-assertion. It is courage spent on others.

For reflection

“Be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.” Which half of that is harder for you? Who are the older men investing in you, and which younger men could you invest in?

6.title: Purity, Work and Finishing Well
6.essay:
Three battlegrounds decide much of a man’s Christian life: sexual purity, daily work and long-term faithfulness. Many men win or lose here.

A covenant with the eyes

Job said, “I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?” (Job 31:1). He did not wait until temptation arrived to decide what he would do. He made a binding promise beforehand. Jesus went further: “everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28).

In a world of instant pornography and constant sexual images, this may be the fiercest battle Christian men face. And it is rarely won in the moment of temptation. It is won by decisions made earlier: where we go, what we watch, what we allow ourselves to look at and dwell on.

Flee and pursue

Paul gives Timothy a two-part strategy: “So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart” (2 Timothy 2:22). Flee: do not negotiate with sexual temptation, but run from it, as Joseph ran from Potiphar’s wife. Pursue: chase something better. The Christian life is not only saying no. It is saying yes to righteousness, faith, love and peace. And notice the last phrase. Purity is a team effort. Men who try to fight alone usually lose.

Purity is more than avoiding certain acts. “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor” (1 Thessalonians 4:3–4). It means honouring God with the body, honouring women as sisters and image-bearers, and keeping sex for the covenant of marriage.

Practical wisdom

Put filters and accountability on your devices. Do not take your phone to bed. Know your danger times: late at night, or when tired, lonely or stressed. Replace, do not only remove: fill your mind with Scripture and your life with good work and friendship. When you fall, confess quickly to God and to a brother, and get back up.

Many men carry deep shame about sexual sin. The gospel does not excuse sin, but it does forgive it. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Shame drives men into hiding. Grace brings them into the light.

Work as worship

“Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). Paul first wrote these words to slaves, people with the hardest and least rewarded work imaginable. Even there, work could be done for the Lord. No job is too small to be done for Christ, and none too important to be done for yourself. Then Paul adds, “You are serving the Lord Christ” (Colossians 3:24). A man’s real boss is Jesus, and Jesus sees what no manager notices.

Work was given before the fall (Genesis 2:15), and Christ himself worked as a carpenter. Whether a man is a labourer, a manager, a student or retired, his work can be worship. It is not merely a way to earn money but a way to serve Christ, love neighbours and provide for others. Laziness is a sin (Proverbs 6:6; 2 Thessalonians 3:10). So is making work an idol that consumes a man’s family and his soul.

Single men

These callings belong to single men as much as married men. Paul says, “The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:32). Singleness is not a waiting room for manhood. It can be a season, or a lifetime, of undivided devotion to Christ.

Finishing well

Many men start strong and fade. Paul, writing from prison and expecting execution, could say, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7). A fight against sin, error and discouragement. A race he did not quit. A trust he guarded. That is how every Christian man should want his life to end: not with perfection, for Paul called himself the foremost of sinners, but with faithfulness, held up to the end by grace.

Men finish well not by gritting their teeth but by keeping their eyes on Christ: “let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus” (Hebrews 12:1–2). Biblical manhood is not a burst of zeal but a long obedience.

An old man who finished strong

At eighty-five, Caleb said to Joshua, “I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me,” and asked for the hardest territory: “So now give me this hill country” (Joshua 14:11–12). He had followed the LORD wholeheartedly for forty-five years. Scripture promises that the righteous “still bear fruit in old age” (Psalm 92:14). Retirement is not the end of a man’s calling. Grandfathers, mentors and praying old men are among the church’s greatest treasures.

For reflection

What practical steps should you take to flee temptation and pursue righteousness with others? Imagine yourself at eighty-five: what kind of man do you want to be then, and what habits now will help you get there?
